The total length of the adult Acreichthys tomentosus rarely surpasses 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], making it a relatively small member of the Monacanthidae family. Population surveys conducted in seagrass habitats throughout the Indo-Pacific indicate that individuals attain a maximal body mass of approximately 65 grams [Wwi = approximately 65 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to field-caught specimens. These dimensions place the species among the smaller leatherjackets, with ultimate size likely constrained by the structural complexity of its preferred algal and seagrass microhabitats. At the onset of reproductive maturity, which occurs after a period of juvenile growth, males and females typically measure about 7 centimeters [Lp = about 7 centimeters] in total length, a figure estimated from comparative data across related filefish species. The corresponding wet weight at this pubertal transition is roughly 8.3 grams [Wwp = roughly 8.3 grams], reflecting a substantial allocation of resources toward somatic development before the first spawning event.

In reproductively active Acreichthys tomentosus, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached 15% [GSI = 15%] at a constant water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. This index, which describes the proportional investment of body mass into ovarian tissue, was established through comparison with the closely related species Thamnaconus modestus and suggests a moderate reproductive allocation strategy. At this temperature, the yolk-sac larvae emerge from their adhesive demersal eggs with a minuscule wet weight of only 0.000097 grams [Wwb = 0.000097 grams], a value calculated from the egg diameter of 0.57 millimeters reported for Stephanolepis hispidus. This extremely small neonatal mass indicates that the newly hatched yolk-dependent larva depends entirely on its yolk reserves during the first days following chorion rupture, before the onset of exogenous feeding and swim bladder inflation.

Under the stable thermal conditions characteristic of its tropical habitat, here approximated by a water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for Acreichthys tomentosus in the wild reaches ten years [am = ten years]. This longevity is remarkable for a fish of such modest adult dimensions, as individuals weighing up to 65 grams [Wwi = up to 65 grams] typically exhibit shorter life expectancies among related monacanthids. The extended lifespan likely reflects the species’ low natural mortality rate in structurally complex seagrass meadows, where dense vegetation provides refuge from piscivorous predators. Seasonal reproductive cycles and a relatively slow growth trajectory allow these individuals to persist for a decade, a duration that mandates multiple spawning events across consecutive breeding seasons to sustain population stability. The life history strategy thus appears to be one of moderate reproductive investment spread over many years rather than a single, high-output episode.

At the point of sexual maturation, the wet weight of an individual rising to first reproduction is approximately 8.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 8.3 grams], equivalent to a total body length of about 7 centimeters [Lp = about 7 centimeters]. This transition from the immature to the reproductively viable stage marks a critical juncture in the life cycle, as the juvenile fish must have accumulated sufficient endogenous energy stores to support the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation. The total length recorded at this milestone represents roughly half the ultimate adult length of 14 centimeters [Li = 14 centimeters], indicating that somatic growth continues to be energetically significant even after reproductive competence is achieved. Spawning adults thus face a trade-off between further increases in body size, which may enhance fecundity in later breeding events, and the immediate costs of gamete production. The moderate wet weight at puberty suggests this species allocates a balanced proportion of its metabolic resources toward both current and future reproductive episodes.

Fertilised eggs of Acreichthys tomentosus, deposited as adhesive, demersal clutches onto seagrass blades, give rise to prolarvae that weigh an average of 0.000097 grams [Wwb = 0.000097 grams] immediately following eclosion. This extremely low hatchling mass is consistent with the pelagic egg diameters observed across the Stephanolepis lineage, and the subsequent endotrophic phase is brief, lasting only until the yolk sac is fully resorbed. Field observations at a water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C] indicate that the gonadosomatic index for mature females reached 15% [GSI = 15%] through the peak spawning season. The maximum lifespan of this species can extend to a full decade (10 years) [am = 10 years] at a temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. These traits collectively sustain the population across heterogeneous reef environments.
